usage: praising a clean, minimal look; 하다-adjective, so 단순하 + 여요 → 단순해요
noun-modifying form is 단순한 + N, never 단순하는
단순한 = 'mere/plain', softening the error as not deep or malicious
Don't think about it too simply
단순하게 = adverb; casual 반말 warning not to oversimplify
examples: 이 앱은 화면이 단순해요.
This app's screen is simple.
plain statement; 단순하다 praises an uncluttered interface
저는 성격이 단순한 편이라 뒤끝이 없어요.
I have a pretty simple personality, so I don't hold grudges.
단순한 + 편이다 = 'on the simple side'; describes an easygoing, low-drama nature, not low intelligence
원인이 생각보다 단순해서 금방 고쳤어요.
The cause was simpler than expected, so I fixed it quickly.
단순해서 = 아서/어서 reason; real troubleshooting reassurance
nuance: 단순(單純) literally combines 單 'single' + 純 'pure', so the core image is 'one pure thing, nothing extra'. It means simple, plain, or uncomplicated in structure or design and is normally positive or neutral. The near-synonym to keep apart is 간단하다(簡單): 간단하다 stresses that a task is quick and brief to do (간단한 점심, 간단히 설명하다), while 단순하다 stresses that a thing's makeup is plain with few parts (단순한 구조). It is a 하다-adjective, so the 요-form is 단순해요 and the modifier is 단순한. Applied to a person, 단순하다 means easygoing and uncomplicated, NOT dumb. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing the English insult 'he's simple' to mean stupid: 단순한 사람 actually sounds like a refreshingly drama-free person; for 'dumb' Koreans add words and say 머리가 단순하다 or 단순무식하다.

mistakes: Swapping 간단하다 and 단순하다 freely. 간단한 식사 (a quick, light meal) cannot become 단순한 식사 without sounding odd, because 단순하다 describes plain structure, not brevity of effort. Use 간단하다 for quick/brief, 단순하다 for plain/uncomplicated.
Saying 단순한 사람 to call someone stupid. To a Korean ear it praises an easygoing, grudge-free personality. For 'dumb' you must say 머리가 단순하다 or 단순무식하다.
Conjugating it like a verb (단순하다고 생각하는 사람 is fine, but 단순하는 구조 is wrong). As an adjective the present modifier is 단순한, never 단순하는.

english: to be dense, finely-spaced, tightly woven
usage: 촘촘한 + N; the teeth sit very close with tiny gaps
촘촘하게 = adverb; habitual partner of 짜다(weave/knit)
small even gaps between threads; nothing slips through
figurative: a thorough plan with no loose gaps
examples: 모기장 구멍이 촘촘해요.
The mosquito net's holes are fine.
plain description; tiny, evenly spaced gaps
이 니트는 촘촘하게 짜여서 따뜻해요.
This knit is densely woven, so it's warm.
촘촘하게 짜이다 = passive 'to be woven tightly'; classic clothing comment
계획을 너무 촘촘하게 세웠더니 쉴 틈이 없었어요.
I planned things so tightly that there was no room to rest.
figurative; -았더니 reports the consequence of an over-detailed plan
nuance: 촘촘하다 is a native Korean (고유어) word, often felt as the doubled 촘촘 'close-close', describing units packed very near each other with tiny, EVEN gaps: comb teeth, mesh, knit stitches, dotted print, or a finely detailed plan. Its tone is usually positive, carrying a sense of fineness and thoroughness. The synonym to contrast is 빽빽하다: 빽빽하다 stresses crowded fullness with no room to breathe and is often slightly negative (빽빽한 지하철), whereas 촘촘하다 stresses small regular spacing and craftsmanship (촘촘한 그물). The opposite is 성기다 / 듬성듬성하다 (sparse, gappy). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'dense' and landing on 빽빽하다 for everything: a fine-toothed comb or tightly knit fabric is 촘촘하다, not 빽빽하다, and big things crammed together (a packed train) are 빽빽하다, not 촘촘하다.

mistakes: Using 촘촘하다 for large objects crowded together, e.g. 사람이 촘촘하다 for a packed crowd. People packed in are 빽빽하다; 촘촘하다 fits small repeated units like teeth, threads, stitches, dots.
Treating 촘촘하다 and 빽빽하다 as identical. 촘촘하다 = fine, even, often praised spacing; 빽빽하다 = crammed with no room, often a complaint. A tightly knit sweater is 촘촘한 니트, not 빽빽한 니트.
Pairing it with the wrong verb. The natural collocation is 촘촘하게 짜다/심다 (weave/plant densely); 촘촘하게 많다 is unnatural.

usage: the fit is too loose around the body
헐렁한 + N; can be an intentional oversized style
헐렁하게 = adverb; a deliberate relaxed styling choice
non-clothing use for a fitting that has worked loose
examples: 이 티셔츠는 좀 헐렁해요.
This T-shirt is a bit loose.
plain fit comment while trying clothes on
살이 빠져서 청바지가 헐렁해졌어요.
I lost weight, so my jeans got baggy.
헐렁해지다 = 'became loose'; -아지다 marks the change of state, not a permanent trait
문고리가 헐렁해서 곧 빠질 것 같아요.
The door handle is loose, so it looks like it'll fall off soon.
헐렁해서 = reason; shows the hardware sense beyond clothes
nuance: 헐렁하다 is a native Korean word for loose, baggy, or slack — mainly clothes that hang away from the body, but also screws, handles, or fittings that have lost their grip. It is the opposite of 꽉 끼다 (skin-tight) and 빡빡하다 (stiff/resistant). The synonym worth separating is 넉넉하다: 넉넉한 옷 is pleasantly roomy with comfortable margin (a compliment), while 헐렁한 옷 leans toward too-loose, sloppy, or oversized. Figuratively 헐렁하다 can paint a person as lax and careless (성격이 헐렁하다 = laid-back to the point of unreliable). The big English-speaker pitfall is using 넓다 for loose clothing because English 'wide/loose' blur together: 넓다 means wide in AREA (a wide road, a wide room), so 바지가 넓다 sounds like the trousers cover a large floor area; loose FIT is 헐렁하다. Also remember 헐렁해지다 for 'became loose' — bare 헐렁했다 implies it was always baggy.

Treating 헐렁하다 as a pure compliment. For a flattering 'nicely roomy' fit, Koreans prefer 넉넉하다; 헐렁하다 often implies it's looser than ideal.

english: to be tight, stiff, packed; (schedule) hectic
usage: the most common figurative use: no spare time
the door is stiff (hard to open)
physical resistance when you push or slide it
빡빡한 + N; back-to-back with no breaks
barely enough money to cover everything
examples: 서랍이 빡빡해서 잘 안 열려요.
The drawer is stiff, so it doesn't open well.
physical sense; 빡빡해서 = reason for the resistance
오늘 회의가 많아서 일정이 빡빡해요.
I have lots of meetings today, so my schedule is packed.
the everyday office use; 일정이 빡빡하다 is a fixed collocation
월세 내고 나면 생활비가 빡빡해요.
After paying rent, my living budget is tight.
money sense; -고 나면 = 'once I've done'; very relatable for residents
nuance: 빡빡하다 is a colloquial native word built on the tense, forceful sound 빡, and it splits into two everyday senses: physically tight and stiff (a drawer, screw, or door that RESISTS moving) and figuratively tight (a packed schedule or a barely-sufficient budget). In both, the core image is zero slack, no breathing room. The synonym to separate is 빠듯하다: 빠듯하다 leans on 'only just enough, cutting it close' (시간이 빠듯하다 = we'll barely make it), while 빡빡하다 adds a feeling of pressure, stiffness, and friction. Don't confuse it with the slang 빡세다, which means an activity is physically or mentally grueling/hardcore (운동이 빡세다), not 'tightly packed'. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'tight schedule' onto 좁다: 좁다 is narrow in physical SPACE (a narrow alley), so 일정이 좁다 is wrong; a tight schedule is 일정이 빡빡하다. Likewise a tight budget is 예산이 빡빡하다, not 예산이 좁다.

Overusing it in very formal writing. 빡빡하다 is casual-to-neutral spoken Korean; in a stiff report you might prefer 빠듯하다 or 여유가 없다.

usage: 매끄러운 + N; ㅂ → 우 before the modifier 운
figurative: deal with something without friction or conflict
of an event or process running without hitches
examples: 이 종이는 표면이 매끄러워요.
This paper has a smooth surface.
plain touch description; note 매끄러워요, not 매끄럽어요
로션을 발랐더니 피부가 매끄러워졌어요.
After I put on lotion, my skin became smooth.
매끄러워지다 = change of state, still ㅂ-irregular; -았더니 reports the result
발표가 매끄럽게 끝나서 다행이에요.
I'm relieved the presentation ended smoothly.
figurative: a polished, hitch-free flow; 매끄럽게 = adverb
nuance: 매끄럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the ㅂ becomes 우/워, giving 매끄러워요, 매끄러운, 매끄러우니까, 매끄러워서 — memorize the 요-form 매끄러워요 and the rest follows. It means smooth and frictionless to the touch (skin, paper, fabric, a polished floor) and figuratively a process or speech that flows without awkward bumps. The crucial synonym contrast is 미끄럽다: both come from the same 'slip' family, but 매끄럽다 is the pleasant, sleek 'smooth to the touch' (a compliment for skin), while 미끄럽다 is the dangerous 'slippery, slip-prone' (a warning about a wet floor). Saying the bathroom floor is 매끄러워요 sounds like you admire its sleek finish; to warn someone they might slip you must say 미끄러워요. The English-speaker pitfall is the regular conjugation 매끄럽어요 — wrong; it must be 매끄러워요, because all ㅂ-irregular adjectives like 춥다→추워요 and 무겁다→무거워요 behave this way.

mistakes: Conjugating it regularly as 매끄럽어요 / 매끄럽은. As a ㅂ-irregular it is 매끄러워요 and 매끄러운, exactly like 춥다 → 추워요 → 추운.

Using it only for physical surfaces. 매끄럽다 also describes a smooth process or delivery — 일을 매끄럽게 처리하다, 발표가 매끄럽다.

usage: ㄹ-stem: 거칠 + 어요 → 거칠어요 (ㄹ kept before 어)
거친 + N; the ㄹ DROPS before ㄴ → 거친, not 거칠은
the way of speaking is harsh
figurative: blunt, rough manner of speech
거칠어지다 = change of state from smooth to rough
examples: 이 수건은 좀 거칠어요.
This towel is a bit coarse.
plain texture comment; not soft against the skin
겨울이라 손이 거칠어져서 핸드크림을 자주 발라요.
It's winter, so my hands get rough and I use hand cream often.
거칠어지다 = becomes rough; -아서/어서 chains the reason
그 사람은 말투가 거칠지만 마음은 따뜻해요.
That person speaks harshly, but has a warm heart.
figurative; -지만 contrasts the rough manner with the kind nature
nuance: 거칠다 is a native ㄹ-stem (ㄹ-탈락) adjective meaning rough or coarse to the touch (skin, towels, unfinished surfaces) and, figuratively, harsh or rough in manner (말투가 거칠다, 운전이 거칠다, 숨이 거칠다). It is the antonym of 매끄럽다 and 부드럽다. The synonym to contrast is 까칠하다: 까칠하다 is a smaller, prickly roughness — slightly stubbly skin, OR a person who is touchy and prickly in temperament (성격이 까칠하다) — whereas 거칠다 is broader and rougher, covering coarse texture and genuinely harsh, wild behavior. The grammar pitfall English speakers hit is the ㄹ-stem rule: the ㄹ DROPS before ㄴ, so the present modifier is 거친 손, never 거칠은 손; but it STAYS before 어, giving 거칠어요. A second pitfall is limiting it to texture — in English 'rough' splits into many words, but 거칠다 naturally also covers harsh speech and aggressive, reckless driving (난폭운전).

Confusing 거칠다 with 까칠하다 for personality. 까칠하다 = touchy, prickly, hard to please; 거칠다 = harsh, wild, rough-mannered. They paint different characters.

usage: typically after touching something sugary or sweaty
humid, clammy summer air clinging to the skin
examples: 음료수를 쏟아서 식탁이 끈적해요.
I spilled a drink, so the table is sticky.
everyday cleanup scene; 끈적해서 also works for the reason
여름엔 습해서 몸이 끈적해요.
In summer it's humid, so my body feels sticky.
끈적하다 for sweaty, clammy skin — a core Korean-summer word
이 로션은 발라도 안 끈적해서 좋아요.
This lotion isn't sticky even after applying, so it's nice.
-아도 = 'even if'; a standard cosmetic-review point
nuance: 끈적하다 (and its lively variants 끈적거리다, 끈적이다, 끈적끈적하다) is a native word for a sticky, tacky, clinging feel: spilled drinks drying on a table, sweat on a humid day, gooey residue, or honey on the fingers. For Korea's muggy summers it perfectly captures clammy skin and 끈적한 날씨. The doubled 끈적끈적하다 amps up to a heavier, syrupy stickiness. The key synonym contrast is with 미끄럽다 (slippery): they are near-opposites in physics — 끈적하다 GRIPS and clings so things stick together, while 미끄럽다 is frictionless so things slide apart. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing texture with taste: English 'sweet and sticky' bundles them, but in Korean 끈적하다 is purely the sticky TEXTURE, and 달다 is the sweet TASTE — a honey-coated table is 끈적하다, the honey itself is 달다. Figuratively 끈적한 시선/관계 can also mean an uncomfortably clingy gaze or relationship.

english: to be densely packed, crammed, dense
usage: crammed so there's no room to move
빽빽한 + N; trees standing close together
tightly written with little spacing between lines
빽빽하게 = adverb; fixed pair with 들어차다(be filled)
examples: 출근 시간 지하철은 사람이 빽빽해요.
The subway at commute time is packed with people.
a very relatable Seoul commute; 사람이 빽빽하다 is a set phrase
수첩에 일정이 빽빽하게 적혀 있어요.
The planner is crammed full of appointments.
빽빽하게 적히다 = densely written; figurative packed schedule
나무가 빽빽해서 햇빛이 잘 안 들어와요.
The trees are dense, so sunlight barely gets in.
빽빽해서 = reason; nature/forest sense
nuance: 빽빽하다 is a native word, felt through the tight, stuffed sound 빽, meaning crammed full with almost no gaps: a packed subway, a dense forest, lines of tiny text squeezed onto a page. Its emphasis is crowdedness and lack of room, and it often carries a slightly oppressive, uncomfortable tone. Contrast it carefully with 촘촘하다 and 복잡하다. Versus 촘촘하다: 촘촘하다 admires fine, even, deliberate spacing (a finely woven net), while 빽빽하다 just stresses 'stuffed full, no space' (a forest you can't walk through). Versus 복잡하다(複雜): 복잡하다 means complicated or chaotically busy in arrangement (복잡한 절차, 복잡한 길), whereas 빽빽하다 is specifically about physical density. The opposite is 한산하다 (deserted, sparse) or 듬성듬성하다. The English-speaker pitfall is using bare 많다 for a crowd: 사람이 많다 just says 'there are many people', while 빽빽하다 adds the crucial nuance of being packed in with no breathing space.

english: to be spacious, roomy, nice and wide
usage: pleasantly roomy, with a positive feel
널찍한 + N; sounds inviting and comfortable
to settle into a roomy spot
easy to park because there's plenty of space
examples: 이 카페는 자리가 널찍해요.
This cafe has roomy seating.
plain praise; a popular cafe-hunting criterion in Korea
원룸치고 화장실이 널찍해요.
For a studio, the bathroom is quite spacious.
N치고 = 'considering it's a ~'; a house-hunting compliment
거실이 널찍해서 가구를 더 놓을 수 있어요.
The living room is roomy, so I can fit more furniture.
널찍해서 = reason; -을 수 있다 shows the practical payoff
nuance: 널찍하다 is a native word derived from 넓다 (wide) plus the suffix -찍하다, which adds a warm, satisfied 'pleasantly so' nuance — so it means not just wide but comfortably, generously roomy, almost always a compliment. The synonym to keep distinct is plain 넓다: 넓다 is the neutral, measurable 'wide/large in area' (운동장이 넓다), while 널찍하다 layers on the feeling that the space is enjoyably spacious and comfortable. You'd use 널찍하다 when house- or seat-hunting to say a place feels nice and open, not merely big. Its direct opposite is 비좁다 (cramped). The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 넓다 for everything because English 'spacious' and 'wide' overlap: if you want the cozy, appreciative 'nice and roomy', 널찍하다 carries it, whereas 넓다 can sound flatly factual. Watch the spelling too — it is 널찍하다, not the common misspelling 넓직하다, even though it comes from 넓다.

english: to be cramped, too narrow, tight on space
usage: feels too small for what it's used for
비좁은 + N; barely room to pass
비좁게 = adverb; squeezed into too little space
uncomfortably tight, e.g. on a bus or plane
examples: 엘리베이터가 비좁아요.
The elevator is cramped.
plain complaint; everyday apartment-building scene
짐이 많아서 원룸이 너무 비좁아요.
I have a lot of stuff, so the studio feels really cramped.
비좁다 stresses 'uncomfortably tight', stronger than plain 좁다
식당이 비좁아서 옆 사람이랑 부딪혔어요.
The restaurant was so cramped I bumped into the person next to me.
비좁아서 = reason; concrete tight-space frustration
nuance: 비좁다 is a native word: the intensifying prefix 비- attaches to 좁다 (narrow) and pushes it to 'so narrow it's uncomfortable', i.e. cramped. It is stronger and more clearly negative than plain 좁다, which can be a neutral statement of size (좁은 방 = a small room). Use 비좁다 for rooms stuffed with belongings, packed elevators, tight restaurant tables, or cramped seats. It is the direct antonym of 널찍하다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold. First, treating 비좁다 and 좁다 as identical: 좁다 just says 'narrow/small', while 비좁다 adds 'too tight for comfort', so a tiny but tidy room can be 좁다 yet only an over-stuffed, uncomfortable one is really 비좁다. Second, borrowing the English metaphor 'narrow-minded' onto this word: a narrow-minded person is 속이 좁다 / 마음이 좁다, never 비좁다 — 비좁다 is strictly about physical space.

Applying it to a narrow long shape that isn't uncomfortable. A slim margin or thin strip is 좁다; reserve 비좁다 for spaces that feel oppressively tight to be in.

usage: comfortable to sink into with a springy give
푹신한 + N; soft and inviting to sit on
doubled form intensifies to extra-soft and bouncy
soft sole that absorbs impact when walking
examples: 호텔 베개가 푹신해요.
The hotel pillow is fluffy.
plain comfort comment; soft with pleasant give
이 운동화는 밑창이 푹신해서 발이 편해요.
These sneakers have a cushiony sole, so my feet are comfortable.
밑창(sole) + 푹신하다; -아서 chains the reason — a common shoe-shopping line
새로 산 매트리스가 너무 푹신해서 허리가 좀 아파요.
The new mattress is too soft, so my back hurts a bit.
너무 푹신하다 shows over-softness can be a downside, not always praise
nuance: 푹신하다 (often doubled to 푹신푹신하다 for emphasis) is a native word built on the soft, sinking sound 푹, describing a soft, springy, cushiony feel with pleasant GIVE when you press it: beds, sofas, pillows, thick cushions, padded shoe soles, fluffy bread. Its opposite is 딱딱하다 (hard/firm). The synonym to separate is 부드럽다: 부드럽다 is smooth and gentle to the touch — about surface softness (부드러운 천, 부드러운 머릿결) — whereas 푹신하다 is about volumetric springiness, how something cushions and bounces back when compressed. A silk scarf is 부드럽다 (smooth) but not 푹신하다; a marshmallow pillow is both. For Koreans shopping for furniture, bedding, or shoes, 푹신하다 is a go-to comfort word. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 'soft = always good': a mattress described as 너무 푹신하다 (too soft) is a complaint, because excessive softness lacks support and can hurt your back — Koreans often prefer something 적당히 단단한 (moderately firm).

Assuming 푹신하다 is always positive. 너무 푹신한 매트리스 is a criticism — too soft, no support, sore back. Context decides whether it's praise.
Using it for a flat, firm surface. A thin yoga mat or hardwood floor is not 푹신하다; the word needs noticeable cushioning and bounce-back.

english: to be damp, soggy, soft from moisture
usage: lost its crispness after absorbing humidity
눅눅한 + N; not fully dried, still clammy
눅눅해지다 = change of state from crisp/dry to damp
examples: 과자가 눅눅해요.
The crackers have gone soggy.
plain statement; the crunch is gone
과자 봉지를 안 닫아서 눅눅해졌어요.
I didn't seal the snack bag, so it went soggy.
눅눅해지다 = 'became soggy'; -아서 chains the cause
장마철엔 빨래가 눅눅해서 잘 안 말라요.
During the rainy season, laundry stays damp and won't dry well.
장마철 context; 눅눅해서 = reason — a classic Korean monsoon problem
nuance: 눅눅하다 is a native word for things that have absorbed moisture and turned damp, soggy, or limp: crackers and seaweed (김) that lost their crunch, laundry that stubbornly won't dry, a humid basement room, a 장마철 (rainy-season) apartment. It is essential vocabulary for Korea's sticky summers. Its opposite is the crisp/dry 바삭하다 (crispy) for food and 보송보송하다 (dry and fluffy) for textiles. The synonym English speakers most often confuse it with is 축축하다: 축축하다 is actively WET to the touch — there is visible or palpable water, like a wet towel or rain-soaked socks — whereas 눅눅하다 is the subtler, stale 'humidity-soaked, limp, no longer crisp' state where nothing is dripping but everything feels clammy and soft. A second pitfall is reaching for 젖다 (to get wet): soggy-from-humidity crackers are 눅눅해졌다, not 젖었다, because 젖다 implies they got splashed or soaked in liquid, not slowly softened by moist air.
